steps.prompt: Where does a word like sometimes or often go?
options: Before the main verb, but after am / is / are
At the end of the sentence, always
steps.answer: Before the main verb, but after am / is / are
steps.why: He sometimes thinks (before the verb) but It is often (after be).

steps.title: Adverbs of frequency
steps.html:
AdverbPositionExample
alwaysbefore the main verbI always get up at six.
usuallybefore the main verbShe usually works at home.
oftenbefore the main verbWe often go to the gym.
sometimesbefore the verb, or firstSometimes I stay in.
rarelybefore the main verbHe rarely goes out.
neverbefore the main verbHe never does housework.
with beafter am / is / areI am never late.

One-word adverbs (always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, never) go before the main verb.

With am / is / are they go after the verb: She is always busy.

Expressions of frequency (every day, once a week, twice a month, three times a year) go at the end of the sentence: He goes to the gym twice a week.

Never is already negative. Say I never do housework, not I don’t never do housework.

steps.title: A day in three lives
steps.html:
Three people, one working week.

Reading

Aliya is a night nurse. She gets up at four in the afternoon and has breakfast when other people are having dinner. She never does housework before work; she does it on Sunday morning, when the rest of the city is asleep. “I always make a to-do list on Saturday,” she says. “Without it, I forget everything.” She goes to the gym twice a week, usually at midnight, because the gym near the hospital never closes.

Tomas is a freelancer. He works at home, so his day has no shape until he gives it one. He starts at nine, stops at one, and goes running for forty minutes. In the afternoon he answers emails and does the shopping. He rarely stays in for the whole evening: three or four times a week he chats with friends online, and once a week he plays chess in a café near his flat. “I don’t have colleagues,” he says, “so I make plans with people. It is work, in a way.”

Ravil is a farmer. His day starts at half past four and it is the same every day of the year. He does some exercise without thinking about it — he walks fifteen kilometres before lunch. He almost never goes to bed late, and he has a lie-in only twice a year. His children do their homework at the kitchen table while he reads the weather report. “People think we live outdoors,” he says. “In winter we live indoors, like everybody else.”

Three days, three shapes. Which one looks most like yours?
